question: When Church, kings and merchants start to write fats down, what do their rules and ledgers show about oil, butter and the whale?
thesis: From 1000 to 1500 fat becomes documented, countable and rule-bound. In Latin Europe the Church’s fasting year splits the continent between butter and oil and turns butter into a matter of dispensations; the Geniza shows oil as an everyday long-distance trade of the Islamic Mediterranean; Song and Yuan China make oil one of the city’s necessities; and the Basques begin to hunt whales for fat.

big_ideas.title: Lent divides Europe into butter and oil
big_ideas.text: Christians fast for about half the year, and the rule bears very differently on a south that has olive oil and a north that has only butter. Councils forbid butter in Lent, a Breton queen lobbies Rome for a dispensation, and a cathedral tower is said to be paid for by butter sinners. Meanwhile butter becomes an everyday fat as English dairying shifts from sheep to cattle.

big_ideas.title: The Geniza makes oil a trade you can count
big_ideas.text: A Tunisian merchant tells of five thousand dinars of oil in Palermo, Alexandria imports five thousand skins from Tunisia in a famine, linseed oil goes from Egypt to Syria and Aden, and a synagogue’s monthly lamp-oil accounts survive. Oil is food, light and money for ordinary people.

big_ideas.title: China makes oil a necessity and a technology
big_ideas.text: A Song miscellany ranks a dozen oils with sesame the best, Hangzhou counts oil among its seven necessities, Wang Zhen gives the first description of the oil press, and su, once butter, drifts into animal-fat shortening under the Mongols, whose court physician uses sheep’s tail fat heavily.

big_ideas.title: The sea becomes a fat for fast days
big_ideas.text: The Basques are the first known organised hunters of large whales, selling blubber as ‘Lenten lard’, and kings tax the catch. In the Arctic, Thule hunters burn whale and seal oil in soapstone lamps, though the date of their whaling is contested.

big_ideas.title: Fat travels to the edges of the known world
big_ideas.text: Baghdad-style dishes reach Latin cookbooks with bacon fat for tail fat, Marco Polo is reported to describe sesame in Persia and India, coconut oil arrives in Borneo in a chronicle, and Cadamosto and Pacheco Pereira are the first Europeans to write of West African palm oil.

threads.title: Lent, butter and oil in Latin Christendom
threads.claim: The fasting rules make fat a religious question, and dispensations show butter winning the north.

beats.text: Christians fast on Wednesdays, Fridays, Saturdays and through Lent, about half the year, and the rule bites hardest where there is no oil.
English dairying shifts from sheep to cattle, and butter becomes an everyday fat.
In the south olive oil is so valuable that three to five litres buy a fat hog.
Spain sends olive oil north and takes wool and hides south, a microcosm of butter north and oil south.
The Council of Angers forbids butter in Lent.
Rouen builds its Butter Tower, said to be paid for by those who bought the right to eat butter in Lent.
Anne of Brittany wins leave for butter in Lent, since Brittany has no oil.

threads.title: Oil in the Mediterranean ledgers
threads.claim: The Cairo Geniza shows how oil moved: olive oil from Tunisia, linseed and sesame from Egypt, in small shops and in great partnerships.

beats.text: Egypt’s flax makes linseed oil the common people’s lamp oil.
Linseed oil is exported from Egypt to olive-growing Syria and to Aden.
A Tunisian merchant in Palermo writes of five thousand dinars of oil in partnership with Muslims and Jews.
In a famine an Alexandria merchant counts five thousand skins of Tunisian oil imported in one season.
The Fustat synagogues’ monthly lamp-oil accounts record olive and linseed oil.
A small Fustat shop’s stock includes two jars of linseed oil.
A Muslim scholar warns against sesame oil squirted from the mouths of Jewish cake makers.

threads.title: Song and Yuan China
threads.claim: Oil goes from one of many fats to a daily necessity, with a described technology and a changing butter.

beats.text: The Chi le pien says oil is used everywhere for eating and burning, sesame the best, and lists a dozen others.
The hard oil of the Chinese tallow tree is poured into candles in Guangnan.
Hangzhou’s seven daily necessities include oil, and oil-pressing shops are seen in the city.
Su, once butter, becomes a shortening based on sheep tallow or lard.
Wang Zhen gives the first description of an oil press in Chinese literature.
The Mongol court physician’s dietetics make heavy use of the fat of the fat-tailed sheep.

threads.title: Whales and the Arctic lamp
threads.claim: The first organised hunting of large whales serves fast days, the Crown and the lamp.

beats.text: The Basques hunt the right whale from watchtowers and sell its blubber as Lenten lard.
Thule hunters rely on bowhead whales and burn seal and whale oil in soapstone lamps, though the old story is contested.
Kings tax the whale: Biarritz in 1197, Bayonne in 1261, the royal fish in 1324.

threads.title: Fat at the edges of the known world
threads.claim: Travellers and chroniclers begin to report fats that Europe barely knew.

beats.text: Polynesians settle Hawai‘i and New Zealand with their tree crops.
Marco Polo is reported to describe sesame varieties in Persia and India.
Arab dishes reach Latin cookbooks, with bacon fat in place of sheep’s tail fat.
A Banjarmasin chronicle has a hero bring four Shanghai jars of coconut oil from Surabaya.
Cadamosto and Pacheco Pereira write of palm oil in cooking and for sale on the West African coast.

turning_points.text: Alexandria imports five thousand skins of Tunisian oil.
Butter becomes an everyday cattle fat in England.
The Chi le pien ranks the oils of Song China.
King John taxes the first whales at Biarritz.
Hangzhou counts oil among its necessities.
Wang Zhen describes the oil press.
The Council of Angers forbids butter in Lent.
Cadamosto reports palm oil in West Africa.
Anne of Brittany wins a butter dispensation.

text: Eleven entries on the Church’s fat line and the kings’ whale: Lent, the Council of Angers, Anne of Brittany, the Butter Tower, the Basques and the whale taxes, butter turning into a cattle fat, oil as money, Arab dishes in Latin cookbooks and Spanish oil going north ([[b1]], [[o1]], [[o2]], [[b2]], [[ec1]], [[o3]], [[ec5]], [[ec6]], [[e1]], [[x1]]). Sicily is here too: a Tunisian merchant’s five thousand dinars of oil in Palermo ([[x3]]).

The Geniza: Tunisian oil shipped to Alexandria, Egypt’s flax, linseed and sesame, linseed to Syria and Aden, a Muslim scholar’s remark on Jewish cake makers and a shop’s stock in 1104 ([[ec2]], [[ec3]], [[x2]], [[l1]], [[l2]]). Egypt is filed here by the atlas taxonomy. The synagogue lamp-oil accounts are here too ([[ec11]]). Marco Polo’s sesame of Persia and India is reported at second hand ([[ec13]]).

Song and Yuan China: a dozen oils, the first description of an oil press, Hangzhou’s necessities, tallow-tree candles and su turning into animal-fat shortening ([[th1]], [[te1]], [[ec4]], [[te2]], [[ec8]]). Southeast Asia gets its first entry here: four Shanghai jars of coconut oil in a Banjarmasin chronicle ([[ec10]]). The Mongol court’s physician writes the tail fat of the fat-tailed sheep into his dietetic recipes in 1330 ([[e2]]).

One entry: palm oil on sale along the West African coast in the 1460s–1480s, as two Portuguese-era writers report it ([[ec7]]). The Tunisian oil in [[ec2]] is filed under the Near East because it is shipped to Egypt. Shea, Ethiopia, the Swahili coast and Mali have no entry; the library holds no source for them.

Three entries: Thule hunters relying on bowhead whales and the soapstone lamp across the Arctic ([[ec9]]), a bison bone-grease and pemmican station at the Mitchell Site in South Dakota, about AD 1000 ([[ec14]]), and the Chimú town of Cerro la Virgen in the Moche Valley, whose middens say most of its meat came from camelids rather than fish, despite its fishing families and tools — a self-sufficiency reading that is itself argued against an older state-outpost one ([[ec15]]).

One entry, with a CONTEXT tier: the settlement of Hawai‘i (AD 940–1130) and New Zealand (about AD 1280), where Polynesian-introduced plants such as candlenut serve archaeologists as dating evidence ([[ec12]]). The sources say nothing about oil.

sources.intro: Documents rule this period. The Geniza, the Song miscellany and the Lenten canons are all read through intermediaries — Goitein, Needham and Khosrova — and so inherit their selection.
main: Khosrova, with Flandrin, for Lent and butter ([[b1]], [[o1]], [[o2]], [[b2]]); Mueller for oil as money ([[ec6]]).
Goitein, *A Mediterranean Society* vol. 1, read by OCR, for the Geniza ([[ec2]], [[ec3]], [[x2]], [[l1]]).
Needham, SCC 6.5, for Song and Yuan China ([[ec4]], [[th1]], [[te1]], [[te2]], [[ec8]]).
Ellis for whaling ([[ec1]], [[o3]]); Lynn for palm oil ([[ec7]]).
Goitein again for the shop of 1104 ([[l2]]); museum and encyclopedia pages found by search for the Thule ([[ec9]]).
Goitein vol. II for the Palermo letter and the synagogue accounts ([[x3]], [[ec11]]); Reid for the Borneo chronicle ([[ec10]]); Chang on the Ming reading of su yu ([[ec8]]).
Anderson for the 1330 dietetics ([[e2]]); Kirch for the Polynesian settlement dates ([[ec12]]).
Mortazavian, in Bedigian’s *Sesame* volume, for Marco Polo on sesame, at second hand ([[ec13]]).
Outram’s Exeter project page for the Mitchell Site bone-grease station ([[ec14]]).
contested: The Rouen tower's financing is tradition without accounts ([[b2]]); the date of the Angers canon is not given ([[o1]]).
Mueller's oil-as-money contracts are unnamed ([[ec6]]); the Butter-to-cattle shift is unsourced ([[ec5]]).
The Muslim scholar's remark on Jewish cake makers is hostile testimony ([[l1]]).
The Thule expansion dates and whaling’s role are argued ([[ec9]]).
The Mitchell Site entry rests on the researcher’s own project page, not the peer-reviewed paper itself, which was not fetched ([[ec14]]).
gaps: Medieval Italian, Spanish and Provençal oil trade, and soap guilds, have no primary source here.
Vol. 3 of Goitein and Ibn Butlan, Seth and Ibn al-Baytar on fats were not read.

Africa has one entry (West African palm oil in the 1400s); nothing on shea after Kirikongo, Ethiopia, the Swahili coast or Mali. The Americas have the Thule only; Aztec, Maya and Andean fats, India, Central Asia, Southeast Asia and Oceania have no entry.

how_to_read: Read the thesis and the big ideas first, then the threads: each runs in date order and points to the entries that carry it. Entries that no thread needs are still reached through the regional picture and the lists.
*Order* and *Belief* carry the Lent story; *Economy* and *Exchange* carry the Geniza and the Song. The Nexus ties the fasting rules to the butter dispensations and the whale taxes.
The two halves of the folio (Latin Europe and the Islamic and Chinese worlds) barely touch, and the Overview reads them side by side.

The *picture by region* counts the 29 entries: Europe 11, Near East 7, Far East 7, Africa 1, Americas 2, Oceania 1; none in Worldwide. The Americas and Africa have one entry each, and the Thule date is itself contested.
